documents.title: Guidance on the Use of Generative AI
documents.summary: University IT guidance defining generative AI and listing privacy, accuracy, bias, IP and consent considerations when adopting tools. It routes teaching and learning questions to the Provost's committee, research questions to Research Computing and others to the Information Security Office.
documents.stance_why: The document sets no stance on student AI use. It covers data protection for all users and says teaching and learning use 'is governed by the Provost’s Committee on Generative AI', so the decision is handed to other bodies.

units.why: The sentence sets the guidance's purpose: adopting generative AI tools must serve the intended use while 'protecting University data'. It is a preamble stating purpose and principle, so P56 (institution-wide framework); it commits no one to a specific action, hence informs.
units.anchor: ensuring the intended use is met while protecting University data

units.why: This is a definition: 'Generative AI is a general term for artificial intelligence that creates new content based on patterns'. It sets what the guidance covers, so P61 (define AI and scope).
units.anchor: Generative AI is a general term for artificial intelligence that creates new content

units.why: The sentence widens the scope to AI 'embedded in many commercial products' such as OtterAI, Zoom IQ and Fireflies. It defines which tools fall under the guidance, so P61; P07 (AI built into editors) is about editors and IDEs and does not match as well.
units.anchor: Generative AI is also now embedded in many commercial products
units.fit_note: Scope statement naming AI embedded in commercial meeting and productivity tools, not editors or IDEs.

units.why: This states a fact about privacy: queries 'will be accessible by others using the same tools' because the tools collect and store user input. It explains why data protection matters, so P50 (tools store prompts), modality informs.
units.anchor: queries in generative AI tools will be accessible by others

units.why: The sentence says faculty, staff, students and affiliates 'should not enter institutional data' into tools not validated by the University and lacking the data provider's permission. It restricts data entry to vetted tools, so P50 (protect data, prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: should not enter institutional data into any generative AI tools that have not been validated
units.resolution_why: Coders agreed on P50, should-not and restrict but A set phase general and B during-work. The sentence is an institution-wide data-handling rule for faculty, staff, students and affiliates, not tied to an assignment or course stage, so general.

units.why: The policy ties allowed data to the 'Northwestern University data classification policy', which 'applies to all University data, including research data'. It makes an existing university policy govern AI use, so P77 (comply with existing policy) rather than P50, which is about protecting data generally.
units.anchor: This policy applies to all University data, including research data.
units.frag_start: outlines four levels for University-owned data
units.fit_note: Names the data classification policy (four levels) as the basis for which data may go into AI tools.
units.resolution_why: Found only by A. Checked against the source: under the heading 'Data Approved for Use with Generative AI' the guidance says the data classification policy 'outlines four levels for University-owned data' and 'applies to all University data, including research data', tying which data may go into AI tools to an existing university policy. It is a real, if brief, statement, so kept as P77 with informs.

units.why: Users are told to use the Tools and Use Guidance page 'to find the right AI tool and review what types of data are allowed'. It points to university-vetted tools by data type, so P50 (prefer vetted tools).
units.anchor: find the right AI tool and review what types of data are allowed
units.resolution_why: A coded phase general, B during-work. The sentence points all users to the Tools and Use Guidance page 'to find the right AI tool and review what types of data are allowed'; it is an institution-wide pointer, not a step in coursework, so general.

units.why: The sentence assigns authority: teaching and learning use 'is governed by the Provost’s Committee on Generative AI, in tandem with Northwestern IT'. It says who sets and maintains the rule, so P56 (institution-level framework); it sets no stance itself.
units.anchor: is governed by the Provost’s Committee on Generative AI, in tandem with Northwestern IT.
units.fit_note: Hands teaching-and-learning rules to the Provost's committee rather than stating a framework itself.
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course, B general; both coded P56 and informs. The sentence says teaching and learning use 'is governed by the Provost’s Committee on Generative AI, in tandem with Northwestern IT'. It names who governs and sets no course-stage action, so general.

units.why: This routes research-use questions to Research Computing and Data Services. It governs who handles AI in research, so P62 (research and scholarship); it states no research rule, hence the fit note.
units.anchor: Questions about AI usage pertaining to research applications can be directed
units.fit_note: Only names the support team for research questions; it contains no rule about research use.

units.why: This routes questions on security, privacy, Level 2 or above data and 'evaluation of new third-party AI products' to the Information Security Office. The review of third-party AI products is closest to P65 (vendor review), though no vendor rule is stated.
units.anchor: evaluation of new third-party AI products can be directed
units.frag_start: Questions about AI usage pertaining to information security
units.fit_note: Names the office that evaluates new third-party AI products and handles Level 2+ data questions; no limit on sharing data with vendors is stated.

units.why: The text says AI models 'will invariably tend to suppress less common or marginalized information'. That names a bias harm, so P53 (name bias and harms), informs.
units.anchor: will invariably tend to suppress less common or marginalized information

units.why: The text warns tools 'can hallucinate or make up random data that is not true'. This is the accuracy caution, so P31 (output is often wrong), informs.
units.anchor: make up random data that is not true

units.why: The guidance says tools 'should be periodically re-validated to ensure appropriate responses' where accuracy matters. It asks users to check AI output, so P31 (verify output); the periodic cycle is a detail the type does not capture.
units.anchor: these tools should be periodically re-validated to ensure appropriate responses
units.fit_note: Asks for periodic re-validation over time because models change, beyond one-time checking of output.

units.why: The text requires that 'necessary approvals for use of original works and intellectual property are obtained prior to input into generative AI tools', naming 'original works developed by students' and 'obtained copyrighted material'. It limits what may be put into AI tools, so P49; P52 is about licensing and ownership of AI inputs and outputs, but the rule here is permission before input. Modality must, stance restrict.
units.anchor: Ensure necessary approvals for use of original works and intellectual property are obtained
units.fit_note: Covers approvals for original works, student work, research results and copyrighted material before input, wider than the course materials in P49.
units.resolution_why: A coded P52 (rights in inputs) and phase general; B coded P49 and during-work. The passage is about getting approval before entering works into AI tools, an input-limiting rule that is the core of P49; P52 centers on licensing and ownership of outputs. Kept P49 with a fit note since it extends beyond course materials. Phase during-work because entering works into tools is the act governed.

units.why: The text says 'Users have the right to know when they are using generative AI tools'. That is a transparency right about AI presence, not any listed type (P47 covers instructors disclosing their own AI use), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Users have the right to know when they are using generative AI tools.
units.frag_start: Users have the right to know
units.uncovered_note: Users have a right to know when they are interacting with generative AI so they can make informed choices (informed consent).

documents.title: Generative AI Advisory Committee
documents.summary: Provost-office page describing the AI and Education Advisory Committee, its charge and responsibilities, and the instructional support units. It defers local AI policy to schools and departments.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no AI stance. It describes the committee's charge and says its 'decentralized structure allows schools and departments to craft context-specific guidance', so the decision is delegated.

units.why: The page says the committee 'serves as a strategic body to guide Northwestern's response' to AI in teaching and learning. It states the purpose and scope of the university's AI governance structure, so P56.
units.anchor: serves as a strategic body to guide Northwestern's response to the emergence of artificial intelligence
units.frag_start: The AI and Education Advisory Committee
units.frag_end: as AI and related technologies advance.
units.resolution_why: B also coded the charge sentence on advising the Provost on 'pedagogical issues and resource development related to AI' as a separate P56 unit; A's 'Advise the Provost on matters of local and institutional policy' bullet covers the same rule, so the two were matched and A's wording kept. Both coders agreed on P56; this note records the alignment only.

units.why: The committee must 'Review policies developed by the Office of the Provost and related units', a standing review duty. It is closest to P54 (revisit policy regularly), though no schedule is given.
units.anchor: Review policies developed by the Office of the Provost and related units
units.fit_note: A standing committee review duty over Provost-office policies; no revision cycle stated.

units.why: The committee must 'Advise the Provost on matters of local and institutional policy' on teaching and learning with AI. It assigns who maintains policy, so P56 (institution-level framework) fits best.
units.anchor: Advise the Provost on matters of local and institutional policy

units.why: The committee will 'Advance instructor engagement through workshops, seminars and conferences'. These are supports for faculty learning about AI, so P63.
units.anchor: Advance instructor engagement through workshops, seminars and conferences
units.resolution_why: A coded phase before-course, B general; both P63, informs. Workshops and seminars to engage instructors on AI are institutional set-up for teaching, so before-course.

units.why: The committee will 'Promote student literacy and responsible use of AI for learning'. This is an AI-literacy aim for students, so P70.
units.anchor: Promote student literacy and responsible use of AI for learning
units.fit_note: States a goal to promote student AI literacy; no training offering or mandate is described.

units.why: The committee will 'Reimagine the future of learning and teaching with AI' by advancing 'leading-edge pedagogical practices'. It is an institutional aim to advance AI-enabled teaching, not a default rule about who may use AI, so P02 does not fit and it is UNCOVERED. Informs, general, encourage.
units.anchor: Reimagine the future of learning and teaching with AI
units.uncovered_note: The committee aims to advance leading-edge AI-based pedagogical practices and classroom environments that foster creativity and engagement. (Coder A had mapped it to P02, noting it is an aim to advance AI-enabled pedagogy, not a default rule about student or instructor use.)
units.resolution_why: A coded P02 (permit or encourage by default) with a fit note saying it is an aim, not a default rule; B coded UNCOVERED. P02 covers a default rule that allows or encourages AI use, and this sentence states no such rule. Following the prefer-UNCOVERED rule, final is UNCOVERED, with A's note kept in the uncovered_note.

units.why: The committee will 'Identify and reduce barriers to instructor adoption of AI by streamlining access to tools, resources and support'. This supports faculty in using AI, so P63.
units.anchor: Identify and reduce barriers to instructor adoption of AI
units.fit_note: Also aims to streamline access to AI tools for instructors.
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course, B general; both P63. Reducing barriers to instructor adoption through access to tools and support is set-up work before courses run, so before-course. B's fit note kept.

units.why: The page lists units offering 'tools, resources and programs tailored to support the thoughtful integration of AI into learning and teaching' (Teaching and Learning Technologies, Libraries, Searle Center). That is institutional support for instructors, so P63.
units.anchor: tools, resources and programs tailored to support the thoughtful integration of AI
units.frag_end: Searle Center for Advancing Learning and Teaching
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course and unit_stance encourage, B general and neutral; both P63 and informs. The sentence lists existing units and their offerings ('offers different tools, resources and programs') without urging anyone, so neutral; phase before-course as instructional support set-up.

units.why: The page says the 'decentralized structure allows schools and departments to craft context-specific guidance'. The university leaves AI rules to schools and departments, so P04 (let each unit or instructor set the rule).
units.anchor: This decentralized structure allows schools and departments to craft context-specific guidance
units.resolution_why: A coded before-course, B general; both P04. The sentence says the structure 'allows schools and departments to craft context-specific guidance', which describes how policy is set up, so before-course.

units.why: The page says 'We encourage instructors to consult with their school and department/program for local policies on the use of AI in teaching.' It sends instructors to local rules instead of setting one, so P04.
units.anchor: We encourage instructors to consult with their school and department/program for local policies

documents.unit: Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences
documents.title: Academic Integrity and Artificial Intelligence: Principles and Guidelines
documents.summary: Weinberg College principles on integrity and AI: passing off AI work as one's own is not allowed, and AI may be used only where instructors permit it and describe the terms. Gives example uses and tells students to ask when unsure.
documents.stance_why: The college says AI 'may be used for coursework only as specifically permitted by instructors', which bans AI unless an instructor permits it.

units.why: The sentence says students 'may not present the work of others, including work generated by artificial intelligence or LLMs, as if it were their own'. That bans submitting AI-generated work as one's own, so P19 (must-not).
units.anchor: students may not present the work of others, including work generated by artificial intelligence
units.frag_end: as if it were their own.
units.resolution_why: A coded phase general, B during-work; both P19, must-not, prohibit. The rule bars students from presenting AI-generated work as their own, an act in submitting work, so during-work.

units.why: The goal of coursework is 'helping students develop the ability to think clearly, logically, and independently'. It gives the learning reason behind the limits, so P41 (practice builds skill), informs.
units.anchor: helping students develop the ability to think clearly, logically, and independently
units.frag_start: Instructors assign academic work for many
units.fit_note: States the goal of coursework generally; the link to AI is made in the next sentence.
units.resolution_why: Found only by A (B coded the separate 'process and product of learning' sentence under P41). Source check: the sentence gives the aim of coursework as 'helping students develop the ability to think clearly, logically, and independently', the goal behind the integrity rule. Real rationale, kept as P41.

units.why: The college says 'we want students to produce academic work in good faith', which 'means that the sources one cites have been directly consulted as part of the process'. Students answer for the integrity of what they submit, so P29 with should; the directly-consulted citation requirement is partly beyond P29.
units.anchor: the sources one cites have been directly consulted as part of the process
units.frag_end: directly consulted as part of the process.
units.fit_note: Good faith includes citing only sources the student has directly consulted.
units.resolution_why: Found only by B. Source check: the passage states what the college wants of student work (good faith, cited sources directly consulted); it is a real expectation, not boilerplate. Kept as P29 with a fit note because the cited-sources condition goes beyond owning submitted work.

units.why: The college wants 'the sources one cites' to have been 'directly consulted', and summaries 'generated by online tools must not replace one’s own research and analysis'. This keeps students as the primary thinker, so P32.
units.anchor: must not replace one’s own research and analysis
units.fit_note: Also requires that cited sources be directly consulted, not taken from AI-generated fragments or summaries.

units.why: Says coursework "always aims to create space for both the process and product of learning" and "the goal is far more than the generation of a final product", a reason to do the work oneself, so P41.
units.anchor: it always aims to create space for both the process and product of learning
units.resolution_why: Found only by B (A coded the earlier sentence on helping students think independently under P41). Source check: 'it always aims to create space for both the process and product of learning. The goal is far more than the generation of a final product' is a distinct rationale sentence for doing the work oneself. Kept as P41.

units.why: The college says LLMs 'cannot always be trusted to deliver accurate information, exhibit true judgment, or be held accountable'. It is a reliability and accountability caution, so P31, informs.
units.anchor: cannot always be trusted to deliver accurate information, exhibit true judgment, or be held accountable

units.why: AI 'can supplement research and learning, but it should not replace the effort that leads to distinctly human discernment'. The limit is justified by the effort that builds judgment, so P41 (AI shortcuts practice that builds skill) with should-not and restrict; P32 is closer to a role rule for the student and this sentence is chiefly a reason.
units.anchor: it should not replace the effort that leads to distinctly human discernment
units.frag_start: AI can supplement research and learning
units.fit_note: Also reads as a rule that students stay the primary thinker (P32).
units.resolution_why: A coded P41, B coded P32; actor, modality and stance agreed. The sentence permits AI to 'supplement' but gives the reason for the limit, the 'effort that leads to distinctly human discernment', which is the skill-building rationale of P41. Kept P41 and recorded the P32 reading in a fit note.

units.why: The guideline says 'artificial intelligence may be used for coursework only as specifically permitted by instructors'. AI is banned unless explicitly permitted, which is the unless-allowed fallback of P06; P01 is a flat default ban and does not capture the permission route. Must-not, restrict, general.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence may be used for coursework only as specifically permitted by instructors
units.frag_start: In the College, artificial intelligence may
units.fit_note: Sets the college-wide default (AI only when specifically permitted by instructors) rather than a rule for silent syllabi; the lifted ban also delegates to instructors (P04).
units.resolution_why: A coded P06, B coded P01 (noting the delegation to instructors); other codes agreed. P06's definition gives the example 'unless explicitly allowed, AI is prohibited', which is this sentence. P01 describes a ban by default without a permission route. Final P06, with both coders' fit notes merged.

units.why: Instructors who allow AI 'should clearly describe in their course policies how students may and may not use AI'. This requires stating expectations in the course policy, so P09.
units.anchor: should clearly describe in their course policies how students may and may not use AI
units.frag_start: Instructors who allow students to use AI
units.frag_end: support or augment their own work
units.fit_note: Applies only to instructors who allow AI, not to every syllabus.
units.resolution_why: Same type, actor, phase and modality; A set unit_stance require, B neutral. The sentence asks instructors to state their AI terms in course policies and takes no position on AI use itself, so neutral. B's fit note kept.

units.why: The text says 'students should adhere to these policies', meaning the instructor's course AI policy. Instructors set the rule and students follow it, so P04 with a student actor.
units.anchor: students should adhere to these policies
units.fit_note: Student side of instructor-set rules: follow whatever the course policy says.

units.why: In courses that allow AI, 'students should be prepared to say how AI was used or consulted.' That asks for disclosure of use, so P24 (disclose with each submission), though no format is given.
units.anchor: students should be prepared to say how AI was used or consulted
units.frag_start: In these courses, students should be prepared
units.fit_note: Requires readiness to say how AI was used, not necessarily a written statement with each submission.

units.why: The sentence says 'it will be important for instructors to be clear about whether AI may be used to support coursework'. This asks instructors to state expectations, so P09 (course-start, should); the mention of AI 'embedded in research and writing tools' is the reason, not a rule on built-in AI, so P07 does not fit as well.
units.anchor: it will be important for instructors to be clear about whether AI may be used
units.frag_start: Given the various ways AI is embedded
units.frag_end: may be used to support coursework.
units.fit_note: Gives AI embedded in research and writing tools as the reason instructors must be clear.
units.resolution_why: A coded P07 (AI in tools); B coded P09. The only directive is that instructors be clear about whether AI may be used, a statement-of-expectations rule. The embedded-tools clause is rationale and sets no rule about such tools. Final P09, with A's point kept as a fit note.

units.why: The guideline gives 'create flash cards or other study tools' as an example of a use that may be appropriate. It allows AI for study aids, so P14.
units.anchor: it may be appropriate to use AI to create flash cards or other study tools
units.frag_start: For example, it may be appropriate

units.why: The guideline says it 'may not be acceptable' in a course allowing some AI 'for students to have AI summarize texts in lieu of reading them'. AI doing the reading in place of the student replaces their own work, so P32 (student stays primary problem-solver) with should-not and restrict.
units.anchor: have AI summarize texts in lieu of reading them
units.frag_start: But it may not be acceptable
units.fit_note: Concerns AI replacing assigned reading, an input to learning rather than a submission; framed as an example an instructor may rule out.
units.resolution_why: A coded UNCOVERED (summaries instead of reading is not submitted work, so not P19); B coded P32. P32 covers students remaining the primary thinker and AI not replacing their thinking, and reading in place of the student is that. Final P32 with a fit note; no new type needed.

units.why: The guideline says it 'may not be acceptable' for students to have AI 'solve problem sets before attempting them'. It protects the student's own first attempt, so P32 with should-not and restrict; P19 is about submitting AI-generated work as one's own.
units.anchor: solve problem sets before attempting them
units.frag_start: But it may not be acceptable
units.fit_note: Ties the limit to order: AI solving problem sets before the student attempts them, not AI use as such.
units.resolution_why: A coded P19, B coded P32. The passage turns on the student attempting the problems first, which keeps the student the primary problem-solver (P32); P19 is about submitted work presented as one's own. Final P32, B's fit note kept.

units.why: The example says it may not be acceptable for AI to 'edit prose for them'. Editing or proofreading the student's text matches P21, though framed as 'may not be acceptable' in a course that allows other uses.
units.anchor: edit prose for them
units.frag_start: But it may not be acceptable
units.fit_note: Concerns editing prose, not code or debugging; it is an example of a use an instructor may rule out, and P21 lists proofreading.
units.resolution_why: Both coders chose P21 (no AI to proofread or check graded work), should-not, restrict. Editing prose is the proofreading/checking use P21 covers. Fit notes merged: it concerns prose, not code, and is an example instructors may rule out.

units.why: The guideline says 'If students aren't sure whether a particular use of AI is appropriate, they should always ask the instructor in advance.' This is the ask-first rule, P10.
units.anchor: they should always ask the instructor in advance
units.frag_start: If students aren’t sure whether a particular use

notes: Reconciled consensus of coder A and B. Course layer deferred; no computing unit found. Provost's Generative AI Policy for Teaching and Coursework (Evanston) was not collected. Topic codes follow the AGENT_BRIEF starter codes.
